intro: Bingley is a town in the Aire valley in West Yorkshire, and above it lies the St Ives Estate, a country park of woods and open moor that Bradford Council has kept open to the public since 1974. A reader walking its woods in November sent us three trees from one corner of it: an old beech with a great broken limb at its foot, a beech forked like a tuning fork, and an Atlas cedar with a twisting second stem. We do not yet know any of their girths.

trees.story:
The St Ives Estate, between Bingley and Harden in West Yorkshire, was a private estate for centuries before Bradford Council took it over in 1974 and opened its woods to everyone. A reader walking there in November sent us this beech.

Among the straight, slim Scots pines it is easy to see why they stopped. The beech is short and thick in the trunk, ribbed and green with moss, and it spreads into a wide crown of fine grey branches that, in the reader's picture, still hold a few copper leaves against a blue sky. It has not had an easy life. A great limb has broken away and lies across the leaf litter at its foot, and their second photograph shows where it tore from the trunk, leaving the wood split open. The tree carries on regardless, its crown still full on the other side.

The reader puts it at 180 to 250 years old. That is their estimate; we have not seen a measurement of its girth or a record of its planting. If you know more about it, tell us here.

Go on a low, late afternoon, as the reader did, when the sun comes through the pines.

trees.story:
A reader in the woods of St Ives, on the edge of Bingley, sent us two photographs of this beech in the late afternoon light, and the second one shows why they stopped.

Most beeches carry one trunk up into the crown. This one splits a little above head height into two stems of the same thickness, which lean apart and then sweep upward again, so that the trunk makes a clean U, a giant tuning fork in grey bark green with moss. Stand at its foot and the pines behind are framed between the two arms. From further back the two stems run up side by side through the bare beeches and the dark Scots pines into one shared crown.

A fork like this often begins when a young tree loses its leading shoot and two side shoots race to replace it. Nobody we know of recorded when that happened here. The reader puts the tree at 100 to 150 years old; that is their estimate, and we have no measurement for it yet. If you measure the trunk below the fork, tell us here.

Stand close to the trunk and look up between the arms.

trees.story:
Atlas cedars come from the mountains of Morocco and Algeria, and they reached English parks with the Victorian taste for trees from far away. A reader walking in St Ives, the old estate on the edge of Bingley that is now a country park, found this one among the native beeches and sent us its photograph.

In November it stands out at once, a dense blue-green crown among bare branches. What makes it worth the walk is the trunk. A straight main stem runs up through the middle, and beside it a second stem leaves the base, bends out sideways, curls back in a long S and only then turns upward to climb into the crown alongside the first, as if it had changed its mind twice on the way.

The reader puts the cedar at 150 to 200 years old. That is their estimate; we have no planting record or measurement for it, and nothing we have read says who planted it. If you know, or have measured its girth, tell us here and we will add it.

Stand at the foot of the trunk and follow the S of the second stem upward.

question_meta: The oldest tree we map in Bingley is a beech on the St Ives Estate, 180 to 250 years old by the estimate of the reader who sent it.
question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Bingley is the Old Beech of St Ives Estate, in the woods of the country park between Bingley and Harden, which the reader who sent it puts at 180 to 250 years old. That is their estimate; we have not seen a measurement. The Atlas cedar a few hundred metres east, at 150 to 200 years by the same reader's estimate, may run it close. The estate is owned by Bradford Council and open all year, free.
question_context: Every age on this page is a reader's estimate, because none of these trees has a published measurement that we know of. All three stand on the St Ives Estate, a country park of about 550 acres between Bingley and Harden in the Aire valley, a former private estate that Bradford Council took over in 1974 and opened to the public. Its woods mix tall Scots pines with broadleaves, and the two beeches and the cedar stand within about three hundred metres of one another among them. The old beech, short and thick in the trunk with a great broken limb at its foot, is the one the reader thinks oldest, at 180 to 250 years. They put the Atlas cedar, with its second stem bending in a long S, at 150 to 200, and the forked beech, whose trunk splits into two equal stems in a clean U, at 100 to 150. A girth would settle more than any of us can from a photograph, so if you walk there with a tape, tell us on the tree's page. The estate is open all year and free, though some routes are signed for walkers only.

faq.q: Where are the trees on the St Ives Estate?
faq.a: In the woods of the St Ives Estate, the country park between Bingley and Harden in West Yorkshire, within about three hundred metres of one another among tall Scots pines. Our pins are approximate, so use each tree's recognition line.
By the estimate of the reader who sent them: 180 to 250 years for the old beech, 150 to 200 for the Atlas cedar and 100 to 150 for the forked beech. We have not seen measurements or planting records.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to visit?
faq.a: No. The St Ives Estate is a Bradford Council country park, open all year and free to walk.
